blocks.h: On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

Classify annuities by commencement (immediate vs deferred), by duration and guarantee structure (whole life, life with guaranteed period, annuity-certain, temporary life annuity), and by the number of lives covered.
Explain the actuarial basis for pricing a life annuity, including the mortality table, the discount rate, the annuity factor, and the natural hedge between life assurance and annuity portfolios.
Describe the structure of the Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS) under the Pension Reform Act 2014: contribution rates, RSAs, PFAs, PFCs, PenCom, and the pension fund investment framework.
Explain the retirement access provisions under PRA 2014: the lump sum right, the 50% minimum pension threshold, and the December 2024 PW template revisions.
Describe the two modes of receiving CPS retirement benefits, Programmed Withdrawal (PW) and Retiree Life Annuity (RLA), including their mechanics, features, guarantees, and limitations.
Conduct a structured comparative analysis of PW vs RLA across income certainty, longevity risk, investment risk, estate benefit, flexibility, inflation protection, and regulatory oversight.
Explain the RLA purchase process: the roles of the PFA, the RLA provider, and the joint PenCom-NAICOM oversight framework.

blocks.h: Every working person faces two fundamental financial risks in retirement. The first, dying too soon, is the risk that life assurance addresses: it pays a lump sum to dependants if the breadwinner dies before financial obligations are met. The second, living too long, is the mirror risk, and in many respects the more insidious of the two. A person who retires at 60 with sufficient savings to last until an expected death at 75 is exposed to serious financial jeopardy if they live to 85 or 90. They will outlive their savings.

An annuity solves this problem by reversing the mortality risk. Instead of paying when the insured dies (as life assurance does), an annuity pays for as long as the insured lives. The annuity contract transfers longevity risk, the risk of unexpectedly long survival, from the individual to the insurer. The insurer, pooling thousands of annuitants, predicts aggregate mortality experience with actuarial confidence and prices its payments accordingly. Those who die early in effect subsidise those who live long, the same pooling mechanism that underlies all insurance, but applied to survival rather than death.

In Nigeria, the annuity market is inextricably linked to the Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS) established by the Pension Reform Act 2014. The CPS mandates that retiring employees either purchase a Retiree Life Annuity (RLA) from a NAICOM-licensed life insurer or remain under Programmed Withdrawal (PW) administered by their Pension Fund Administrator (PFA). The choice between these two modes is one of the most consequential financial decisions a Nigerian worker will ever make.

This chapter equips the practitioner with the theoretical, actuarial, regulatory, and advisory foundations needed to understand, explain, and advise on annuities and retirement income products in Nigeria. It begins with a systematic taxonomy of annuity types, proceeds through the actuarial basis of annuity pricing, maps the Nigerian CPS framework in detail, and provides the comparative analysis of PW and RLA that every practitioner serving retirees must master.

A financial contract under which an insurer undertakes to make a series of periodic payments to an individual (the annuitant) either immediately or from a specified future date. Life annuities are contingent on the survival of the annuitant, payments continue for as long as the annuitant lives and cease on death, unless a guaranteed payment period applies. An annuity transforms a lump sum of capital into a guaranteed income stream, transferring longevity risk from the individual to the pooling institution.
Cf: Life assurance (pays a lump sum on death). An annuity is the economic and actuarial complement of life assurance.
(a) Immediate Annuity

An immediate annuity begins making payments within one payment period of the premium being paid. The annuitant makes a single lump-sum payment to the insurer and receives the first annuity payment almost immediately, typically within one month for monthly annuities. This is the structure used for the Retiree Life Annuity (RLA) in Nigeria: the retiree transfers their RSA balance as a single premium, and the insurer begins making monthly or quarterly payments within the same period.
(b) Deferred Annuity

A deferred annuity postpones the payment commencement to a specified future date, the annuity commencement date (ACD), which may be years after the premium is paid. During the deferral period, the fund grows at a guaranteed rate or in a linked investment account. At the ACD, the accumulated fund converts to an income stream. The Contributory Pension Scheme itself functions as a mandatory national deferred annuity system: contributions accumulate during the working years (the accumulation phase) and the fund is accessed at retirement (the income phase).

RLA purchased with RSA balance at retirement
At a specified future date: years after accumulation
The CPS is a deferred annuity accumulation mechanism; also sold as savings-to-retirement plans
At a future date; accumulation linked to investment fund performance

blocks.h: (a) Whole Life Annuity

A whole life annuity pays an income for the entire remaining lifetime of the annuitant. Payments cease on death. This provides the highest possible income per unit of premium, the insurer has no obligation after death, but leaves no estate benefit if the annuitant dies shortly after purchase.
(b) Life Annuity with Guaranteed Period

To address the perceived unfairness of early death under a pure life annuity, most annuity products include a guaranteed payment period, in Nigeria, 10 years. The insurer guarantees payments for at least the guaranteed period regardless of whether the annuitant dies within it. If the annuitant dies before the end of the guaranteed period, the remaining guaranteed payments are paid to the named beneficiary. After the guaranteed period, payments continue for life. PenCom's CPS framework stipulates the 10-year guarantee for the Nigerian RLA.
(c) Annuity-Certain

An annuity-certain pays for a fixed period regardless of survival. If the annuitant dies before the end of the period, payments continue to the estate or beneficiary. No mortality contingency applies; it is a fixed series of payments with no longevity protection.
(d) Temporary Life Annuity

A temporary life annuity pays for a specified period but only while the annuitant survives. If the annuitant dies before the end of the period, payments cease. Useful for matching a specific finite obligation.
(a) Single-Life Annuity
Written on one life only. Payments contingent on the annuitant's survival. Provides the highest monthly income per unit of premium but leaves a surviving spouse with no continuing income after death.
(b) Joint-Life Annuity

Written on two lives, typically a married couple, paying while both are alive. Payments cease on the first death. Lower income than single-life for the same premium because payments extend until the first of two deaths.
(c) Last-Survivor (Reversionary) Annuity

The most practical structure for couples. Pays a full income while both lives are alive, then a reduced continuation rate (typically 50–66% of the original payment) to the surviving annuitant after the first death, continuing until the survivor's death. The continuation rate is agreed at inception and affects the annuity price.

A joint annuity that pays a full income while both lives are alive and a reduced income (the continuation rate, typically 50–66%) to the surviving annuitant after the first death. Payments continue until the death of the last survivor. The continuation rate determines the price: higher continuation rate = higher annuity premium for the same initial income.
Primary application: Married couples in retirement seeking income continuity for both partners across both lifetimes.

blocks.text: 8.3  The Actuarial Basis of Annuity Pricing

blocks.h: Pricing a life annuity requires the insurer to answer one complex question: given a single premium received today, how large a periodic payment can the insurer guarantee to make for the remainder of the annuitant's life while remaining financially solvent? The answer depends on: the mortality table (how long the annuitant is expected to live), the investment return assumption (the rate the insurer expects to earn on the premium fund), and the expense and profit loading.

The mortality table used for annuity pricing uses lighter (lower) mortality rates than life assurance tables, annuity mortality tables assume annuitants will live longer than the general population. This is because of adverse selection: a person who chooses to purchase an annuity has implicitly bet on living a long time. People who expect to die soon are less likely to buy life annuities. The insurer must price for this self-selected, longer-lived population.

Critically, life assurance and annuity portfolios provide a natural hedge to each other: a year of lower-than-expected mortality (fewer deaths) is good news for annuity portfolios (fewer death claims, more annuity payments required) but bad news for life assurance portfolios. This natural inverse relationship is one reason life insurance companies are the natural and regulatory home for annuity products.

The present value of a periodic payment of ₦1 to a life aged x at an assumed interest rate i, representing the lump sum needed today to fund all expected future payments to the annuitant. In standard actuarial notation, a_x denotes the whole life annuity-immediate factor; ä_x denotes the annuity-due (beginning-of-period payments). The single annuity premium = Desired annual income × Annuity factor. The factor falls as the interest rate rises (higher returns require a smaller fund to support the same income) and rises as the mortality table becomes lighter (longer expected survival requires a larger fund).
See: Dickson, Hardy and Waters, Actuarial Mathematics for Life Contingent Risks (3rd edn, Cambridge, 2020); EFU Life Table (Nigerian standard).

blocks.h: Scenario: A 60-year-old male Nigerian retiree has an RSA balance of ₦15 million after his lump sum withdrawal, to be used as a single premium for an RLA with a 10-year guarantee.
Actuarial assumptions used by the RLA provider:

items.h: Male life expectancy at age 60 (Nigerian EFU Life Table): approximately 20 additional years
Investment return assumption: 12% per annum
Expense and profit loading: 5% of annual annuity payment
10-year guaranteed period built into the product

blocks.h: Simplified annuity factor ≈ 7.5 (present value of ₦1 per year for the expected lifetime at 12% p.a., incorporating both time value and mortality probability, a simplified figure for illustration).
Estimated annual annuity = Premium ÷ Annuity Factor ÷ (1 + expense loading)
= ₦15,000,000 ÷ 7.5 ÷ 1.05 = ₦1,904,762 per year → approximately ₦158,730 per month.

This ₦158,730 per month is guaranteed for at least 10 years. If the retiree dies before age 70, the present value of remaining guaranteed payments is paid as a lump sum to the beneficiary. If the retiree survives to 88 (28 years of payments), total payments received = ₦53.4 million against a ₦15 million premium, the pool funded by those who died early.

Annuity prices are highly sensitive to the assumed investment rate. Higher assumed returns produce higher annuity payments for the same premium; lower returns produce lower payments. This sensitivity creates a market dynamic in Nigeria: during periods of high interest rates (as experienced in recent years with Nigerian government bond yields above 18%) annuity income rates are relatively favourable. When yields fall, annuity rates deteriorate. This also creates a key actuarial risk for the insurer: if actual investment returns fall below the pricing assumption, reserves may be inadequate for all future payments, precisely why NIIRA 2025 requires full actuarial reserving and excludes annuity business from the lower-capitalised Standalone Insurtech category.

blocks.text: 8.4  The Contributory Pension Scheme: Nigeria's Retirement Income Architecture

blocks.h: The Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS) was established by the Pension Reform Act 2004 and re-enacted by the Pension Reform Act 2014. It replaced Nigeria's defined-benefit (DB) pension system (which had accumulated massive unfunded liabilities and failed to pay many retirees) with a privately managed, individually funded defined-contribution (DC) system. Each employee holds their own Retirement Savings Account (RSA), contributed to by both employer and employee throughout the working career. The accumulated fund belongs to the employee and is portable across employers.

Nigeria's mandatory national pension system under the PRA 2014, under which employers (minimum 10%) and employees (minimum 8%) contribute to individual Retirement Savings Accounts (RSAs) managed by licensed Pension Fund Administrators (PFAs). The accumulated RSA balance plus investment returns forms the retirement corpus used to fund post-retirement income either through Programmed Withdrawal or a Retiree Life Annuity.
Minimum contributions: 10% employer + 8% employee = minimum 18% of monthly emoluments (basic salary + housing + transport).

blocks.text: 8.5  Accessing Retirement Benefits Under the CPS
8.5.1  The Retirement Trigger and Lump Sum

blocks.h: Under Section 7(1) of PRA 2014, an RSA holder accesses retirement benefits upon retirement or attaining age 50, whichever is later. At retirement, the holder may withdraw a lump sum from the RSA, provided that the residual amount is sufficient to fund PW or RLA income of not less than 50% of the retiree's last monthly salary.[1]

In December 2024, PenCom issued a revised PW template that removed the previous restriction capping lump sum access at 50% of the RSA balance. Retirees may now access any lump sum amount provided the residual balance still funds the 50% minimum pension threshold. This liberalisation allows retirees with large RSA balances to access more capital for specific needs (home purchase, business investment, debt settlement) while maintaining their minimum ongoing income.[8]

blocks.text: 8.5.2  The Two Modes of Retirement Income

blocks.h: After any lump sum withdrawal, the retiree must choose between two income modes:<sup>[3]</sup>

items.h: Programmed Withdrawal (PW): The residual RSA balance remains with the PFA, which calculates and pays monthly or quarterly pension from the RSA over the retiree's expected lifespan.

Retiree Life Annuity (RLA): The residual RSA balance is transferred to a NAICOM-licensed life insurer as a single annuity premium. The insurer pays monthly or quarterly income for life with a 10-year guarantee.

blocks.h: PenCom's regulations require that PFAs provide the CPS Retirement Pack to employees at least three months before their expected retirement date. No party (employer, PFA, RLA provider, or broker) may compel a retiree to choose either option.

Under PW, the retiree's residual RSA balance remains with the PFA and is transferred to the Retiree Fund (Fund IV), a dedicated, conservatively allocated investment fund. The PFA calculates the monthly or quarterly pension using PenCom's standardised PW template, taking into account the RSA balance, the retiree's actuarial life expectancy, and projected investment returns.<sup>[12]</sup>
The key feature of PW is that the RSA balance is not transferred to a third party; it remains the property of the retiree, managed by the PFA. This means:

items.h: The RSA balance continues to earn investment returns, which may enhance future PW payments if the PFA's Retiree Fund performs well.
If the retiree dies, whatever balance remains is paid in full to the named beneficiary, no forfeiture, no time limit.
The retiree may switch from PW to RLA at any time. The reverse is not permitted.
PW payment levels may be periodically revised, upward if the fund performs well; downward if the fund is depleted faster than expected.

Fund depletion risk: If the retiree lives significantly longer than actuarial expectation, the RSA may be exhausted. PenCom's Guaranteed Minimum Pension (GMP) provides a floor for retirees whose PW falls below one-third of the national minimum wage, but this does not replicate the lifetime income guarantee of an RLA.
Investment risk: PW payments are linked to Retiree Fund performance. A sequence of poor returns shortly after retirement can permanently reduce PW income.
PFA operational risk: If the PFA encounters financial or operational difficulties, PenCom oversight and the PFC's ring-fenced custody structure reduce but do not fully eliminate the risk.

blocks.h: The RLA is a contract between the retiree and a NAICOM-licensed life insurer. The retiree transfers the residual RSA balance as a single premium; the insurer guarantees a fixed monthly or quarterly income for the remainder of the retiree's life, with a minimum 10-year guarantee.<sup>[2]</sup>

items.h: Income for life: Payments continue regardless of how long the annuitant lives. The insurer bears longevity risk.
10-year minimum guarantee: If the retiree dies within 10 years, the present value of remaining guaranteed payments is paid to the named beneficiary as a lump sum.
Fixed nominal amount: Income does not fluctuate with investment performance; it is a guaranteed contractual obligation.
Generally irrevocable: The decision cannot normally be reversed. The retiree may transfer to a different RLA provider after at least two years.
NAICOM product approval required: All RLA products must be filed with and approved by NAICOM. Standalone Insurtechs may not write RLA business under NIIRA 2025.

blocks.h: A contract under which a NAICOM-licensed life insurer receives the residual RSA balance of a CPS retiree as a single premium and undertakes to pay a fixed monthly or quarterly income for life, guaranteed for a minimum of 10 years. If the retiree dies within the guaranteed period, the present value of remaining guaranteed payments is paid as a lump sum to the named beneficiary. Generally irrevocable, transfers longevity risk from the retiree to the insurer.
Regulatory basis: PRA 2014, Section 7(1)(c); PenCom Revised Regulation on Retirement Benefits (2022); NAICOM product approval; NIIRA 2025 (annuity excluded from Standalone Insurtech licences).
The RLA purchase involves a structured workflow between the retiree, PFA, and RLA provider:<sup>[9]</sup>

items.h: Pre-retirement (3 months before): PFA provides the CPS Retirement Pack with SRBC template showing estimated RSA balance, lump sum options, and projected monthly income under both PW and RLA.
Retiree decision: Retiree studies both options and selects voluntarily. Independent financial advice is recommended.

RLA provider selection: Retiree chooses an approved life insurer from NAICOM's register and obtains a provisional RLA agreement showing the monthly income, guarantee terms, and beneficiary designation.
PFA submission: Signed provisional RLA agreement submitted to PFA with required documentation: retirement letter from employer; evidence of age; RSA statement.
Fund transfer: PFA verifies documentation, confirms with PenCom, and transfers the designated RSA balance to the RLA provider as a single premium.
Annuity commencement: RLA provider confirms receipt of premium and commences monthly/quarterly payments, typically within one month of premium transfer.

blocks.h: Scenario 1: Early death (within guarantee): Retired at 60. Monthly annuity: ₦150,000. Died March 2027, 25 months into the annuity. Remaining guaranteed payments: 95 months. Present value of 95 × ₦150,000 at the prevailing discount rate is paid as a lump sum to the named beneficiary. The family still receives significant capital despite the early death.

Scenario 2: Long life (beyond guarantee): Retired at 60. Monthly annuity: ₦150,000. Lives to 88, 28 years of payments totalling ₦50.4 million against a ₦15 million single premium. The insurer meets this obligation from the pooling effect: those who died early in the guaranteed period funded the long-lived annuitants. After death in 2053, the beneficiary receives nothing; the annuity is fully exhausted.

blocks.h: The PW-RLA choice is one of the most consequential financial decisions a Nigerian retiree will ever make. PenCom's own data shows a persistent 3:1 preference for PW. The following table provides a structured comparison across seven key dimensions.

blocks.h: From inception to end-2022, approximately 319,833 retirees chose PW vs 105,047 choosing RLA, a 3:1 preference for PW. This persistent preference is driven by: cultural weight placed on estate inheritance (PW leaves the full RSA balance to beneficiaries at death); limited trust in life insurance institutions; and inadequate financial education about the longevity risk the PW retiree bears.

blocks.title: Advisory: PW vs RLA, A Decision Framework for Practitioners

blocks.h: Practitioners advising retirees on the PW-RLA choice should apply the following structured framework:

items.h: Health and life expectancy: Excellent health and family longevity favours RLA (the lifetime income guarantee is valuable). Serious health conditions favouring short life expectancy favour PW (preserving the RSA balance for beneficiaries).

Other income sources: A retiree with reliable other income (rental, business) can bear PW's longevity risk. A retiree whose CPS pension is their primary income source should consider RLA's certainty carefully.

Beneficiary needs: Substantial dependants (young children, disabled spouse) increase the value of PW's full estate benefit. A retiree with no dependants has less reason to sacrifice the RLA's certainty.

Inflation risk: In Nigeria's high-inflation environment, the fixed nominal RLA income may be inadequate in 15–20 years. Explore whether the chosen RLA provider offers indexed or escalating annuity options.

Insurer creditworthiness: The RLA is only as good as the insurer's financial solvency over 20–30 years. Assess NIIRA 2025 recapitalisation compliance, Agusto & Co. or GCR rating, and claims settlement record before recommending a specific provider.

blocks.h: Legal note: 'The law does not favour either option but preserves retirees' right to make an informed election. The choice should be made deliberately, knowledgeably, and with full appreciation of its legal implications.': Ivo Takor, VP NBA Epe Branch, February 2026.[7]

blocks.text: 8.9  NIIRA 2025: The Regulatory Framework for Annuity Business

blocks.h: Under NIIRA 2025, annuity is one of the four statutory classes of life insurance business. A life insurer must hold specific annuity class authorisation to write RLA products. NAICOM reviews and approves all RLA product terms, pricing structures, and guarantee features before they may be offered to retirees.<sup>[13]</sup>

blocks.title: Regulatory Spotlight: NIIRA 2025, Annuity Business Excluded from Standalone Insurtech Licences

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 specifically excludes Retirement Life Annuity business from the scope of the Standalone Insurtech licence. Only conventional life insurance companies with full NAICOM life insurance licences and annuity class authorisation may write RLA products. The regulatory rationale is compelling:

items.h: Long duration: RLA obligations extend over 20–30 years. The ₦10 billion minimum capital for conventional life insurers reflects this; Standalone Insurtechs (minimum ₦1 billion) are not capitalised for decades of guaranteed annuity payments.

Actuarial complexity: RLA pricing requires mortality modelling, long-term investment return assumptions, and sophisticated reserving, only feasible with a full actuarial function that conventional life insurers maintain.
Longevity risk pooling: Financial sustainability of the RLA depends on pooling a large annuitant population. A new Insurtech with a small book lacks actuarial credibility.
Irrevocability: The retiree cannot exit the RLA if the provider becomes insolvent. The higher capital requirements and supervision of full life insurers are the primary consumer protection.

blocks.h: Implication: Insurtechs may participate in the RLA distribution chain as comparison platforms, digital onboarding facilitators, or customer service interfaces, but may not underwrite any annuity risk. Any attempt to do so would constitute unlicensed insurance under NIIRA 2025.[17]
The administration of RLA products sits at the intersection of pension regulation (PenCom) and insurance regulation (NAICOM). This is managed through joint circulars and agreed protocols:

items.h: NAICOM: supervises the financial soundness of the RLA provider (capital, investment, reserving, solvency) and approves RLA product terms and rates.
PenCom: supervises the retirement benefit administration process, fund transfer from RSA to RLA provider, documentation requirements, and the protection of retirees' rights during benefit election.
A dissatisfied RLA retiree should first complain to the provider, then escalate to NAICOM (product and financial complaints) or PenCom (benefit administration complaints).

blocks.text: 8.10  Disability Income Insurance and the Retirement Lifecycle

blocks.h: A disability income insurance policy pays a regular monthly income if the policyholder becomes unable to work due to illness or injury. Unlike the death benefit of a life policy or the Retiree Life Annuity, disability income insurance is designed for the working years, it replaces income lost due to a disability that prevents earnings. Key structural features:

items.h: Benefit: Typically 60–75% of pre-disability monthly income.
Waiting (deferred) period: 30, 60, or 90 days before benefits begin. Longer waiting period = lower premium.
Benefit period: To age 60 (retirement) or for a specified number of years.

Definition of disability: 'Own occupation' (more favourable to policyholder) or 'any occupation' (more restrictive). Own-occupation definition pays if the policyholder cannot perform their specific duties; any-occupation pays only if they cannot perform any reasonable work.

blocks.h: Understanding annuities in context requires understanding the full retirement lifecycle:

items.h: Accumulation phase (working years): CPS contributions accumulate in the RSA. Voluntary Contributions (VCs) may boost the retirement corpus. PFA investment management compounds returns over 30 years.
Pre-retirement phase (3–5 years before retirement): RSA consolidated. CPS Retirement Pack provided. Lump sum, PW, and RLA options evaluated. Estate planning and beneficiary nominations completed.
Retirement access phase: Lump sum accessed (subject to 50% minimum pension floor). PW or RLA selected and implemented.
Income phase: Monthly income received from PFA (PW) or RLA provider. Supplemented by any other income sources.
Advanced age phase: If PW balance is exhausted, GMP and en-bloc payment provisions apply. RLA retirees continue receiving guaranteed income for life, the product delivers as designed.

An annuity solves the longevity risk problem, the risk of outliving savings, by guaranteeing periodic income for the annuitant's entire lifetime. It is the economic complement of life assurance: where life assurance pays on death, an annuity pays on survival.

Annuities are classified by commencement (immediate vs deferred), by duration and guarantee (whole life, life with guaranteed period, annuity-certain, temporary), and by the number of lives covered (single life, joint-life, last-survivor/reversionary).

Annuity pricing uses lighter mortality tables than life assurance (annuitants self-select for longer lives), a discount rate reflecting investment returns, and expense/profit loadings. The annuity factor is the present value of ₦1 per period for a life aged x at interest rate i. Life assurance and annuity portfolios provide a natural mortality hedge.

The CPS under PRA 2014 is Nigeria's mandatory national retirement system: minimum contributions of 10% employer + 8% employee to individual RSAs managed by PFAs. PenCom supervises; PFCs hold assets; licensed life insurers provide RLA products.

At retirement, RSA holders may withdraw a lump sum (provided the residual funds the 50% minimum pension floor), then choose PW (income from PFA, variable, full estate benefit) or RLA (guaranteed lifetime income from insurer, fixed, 10-year beneficiary guarantee).

From inception to end-2022: 319,833 retirees on PW vs 105,047 on RLA, a 3:1 preference for PW. This reflects estate benefit preferences, limited insurer trust, and inadequate financial literacy about longevity risk.
The RLA is generally irrevocable once executed. A retiree can switch from PW to RLA at any time; cannot reverse from RLA to PW; can transfer to a different RLA provider after 2 years.

NIIRA 2025 excludes annuity business from Standalone Insurtech licences. Only full life insurance licensees with annuity class authorisation may write RLA products. Insurtechs may distribute but may not underwrite annuity risk.
The PW-RLA advisory decision framework considers: health status, other income sources, beneficiary needs, inflation risk tolerance, and the financial strength of the chosen RLA provider.
